newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Aerospace seen boosting Smiths Ind.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Aerospace seen boosting Smiths Ind.

text.p: Avionics to medical and industrial products group Smiths Industries Plc said on Wednesday that stronger demand from aircraft manufacturers helped boost its half-year profits by 15 percent and it expected earnings to continue growing.

Group profits for the six months to February 1 rose to 80.2 million pounds ($130.4 million) from 69.5 million pounds last year on sales up six percent at 495.3 million pounds. An exceptional gain on a property sale added a further 4.0 million pounds to the pretax result.
The dividend was raised 10 percent to 6.15 pence a share in line with market forecasts, on post-exceptional earnings up 22 percent at 18.9 pence a share.
The company said it expected earnings to go on growing, despite a slowdown in growth in the medical products division.
Analysts said the cautious statement about the star-performing medical systems division made some traders nervous and the shares reversed early gains to fall 12 1/2 pence to 783 by 1520 GMT.

"I am slightly at a loss to explain it (the share price fall)," said Nick Cunningham at brokers BZW. "It has to be said that this stock, like all the other highly-rated stocks, is subject to the odd wobble."
"I think there was a bit of overreaction to the fact that medical was flat," he said.
The company said recent strength in sterling had affected British exports in the medical division but margins had improved and its substantial U.S. business "made satisfactory progress".

"Although the company did a very good job of explaining the impact of foreign exchange, I think just to see it in black and white that as a business it didn't grow in the first half was just a bit of a shock for some people," said an analyst who declined to be named.

Smiths said the division, which specialises in single-use products and surgical equipment, was held back by the strength of sterling. But operating margins at the famously profitable division rose to 22.4 percent from 21.6 percent a year ago to leave operating profits up 300,000 pounds at 31.9 million pounds.

"It is a premium margin business," Chairman Sir Roger Hurn said in an interview. "Our policy particularly over this period has been not to chase sales at the expense of margin but to make sure that we make quality sales and maintain margin," he said.
Hurn said the impact of sterling's strength on the group's results was limited because more than half of the company's manufacturing was based overseas.
He estimated that the overall impact was to reduce profits by about two million pounds in translation of foreign earnings and by a further two million due to the medical division's export business.
"I don't think it's a very big effect. We're less effected by this than some other UK-based companies," he said.

The company also said it expected profits to take off in the aerospace division, which was enjoying the beginnings of an upturn in both civil and military aircraft production, particularly at its key U.S. customers Boeing and McDonnell Douglas.

Operating profits at the division rose 5.7 million pounds to 22.9 million in the half year on sales up 12.7 million at 184.1 million pounds, an increase in operating margin of 2.4 points to 12.4 percent.
"At the peak of the last boom (in the aerospace industry cycle) in 1992 we were making between 15 and 16 percent margins. The fact is that this is the start of an upturn," Hurn said.

BZW's Cunningham said that following the results he was contemplating an upgrade of his current year forecast to 196 million pounds for underlying pretax profits from 190 million and to 44.4 pence for earnings from 43.1 pence.
For the 1997-98 year he has pencilled in an upgrade in profits to 220 million pounds from 208 million currently.
"If one makes even very modest assumptions about operational gearing then all of our (analysts') forecasts are far too low and aerospace profits should run away," said Cunningham.
